profile.reading:
Per Flexential's own individual facility page, this building (Flexential Charlotte - South) is located at 8910 Lenox Pointe Drive B, Charlotte, NC 28272. The operator publishes a footprint of 66666 square feet and 2.36 MW of critical load UPS capacity for this specific building, with published certifications and compliance attestations including PCI DSS, SOC 1 Type II, SOC 2 Type II, SOC 3, HITRUST, ISO 27001, SSAE 18. North Carolina's data center demand has grown sharply: Duke Energy's projected additional capacity need rose from about 3.9 gigawatts in early 2024 to nearly 6 gigawatts by May 2025, roughly equivalent to four nuclear plants, according to Canary Media's reporting. Major projects driving that growth include Amazon Web Services' $10 billion, 800-acre campus in Richmond County, billed as the largest single capital project in North Carolina history; an Apple site in Catawba County included in the company's broader $500 billion US expansion; four new Microsoft data centers planned near Charlotte; and an expansion of Google's Caldwell County facility. Duke has won regulatory approval for a large new fleet of gas plants despite state decarbonization requirements, prompting a policy debate among clean-energy advocates who favor load flexibility, utility-scale solar and battery storage, virtual power plants, and clean-transition tariffs as alternatives; a North Carolina Utilities Commission proceeding was scheduled for October 2025 to examine these competing approaches, with timeline pressure driven partly by neighboring Virginia's data center construction pace of 18 months or less.

Duke Energy has separately sought a 15% North Carolina rate increase over two years, on top of bills that had already risen about 22% since 2020, and data centers, currently less than 1% of peak energy use but projected to eventually account for roughly 80% of future demand growth and about 30% of upcoming development projects statewide, have become central to the resulting rate debate, per reporting citing Environmental Defense Fund policy director Will Scott. Scott has argued new power plants built to serve data centers should be paid for through special fees on those large customers rather than socialized across all ratepayers, while Duke spokesperson Bill Norton has disputed that data centers are driving the increases, attributing them instead to infrastructure maintenance and arguing that industrial growth broadly helps spread fixed costs over a larger customer base.

reading.body:
Flexential Charlotte - South publishes 2.36 MW of IT capacity across 66,666 square feet, a small facility by AI infrastructure standards where meaningful training clusters routinely require tens or hundreds of megawatts.

The facility's certification profile points toward compliance-driven enterprise workloads rather than large-scale AI training. SOC 1 Type II and SOC 2 Type II qualify it for financially sensitive enterprise applications. PCI DSS qualifies it for payment card data. HITRUST qualifies it for regulated healthcare information. ISO 27001 and SSAE 18 signal an auditable information security framework. These certifications prioritize regulatory audit posture over the raw power density that foundation model training demands.

Among five facilities in North Carolina that publish megawatt figures, this campus ranks fourth with roughly 4.6 percent of the state's 51.47 MW total published capacity. North Carolina itself remains modest relative to AI-scale deployments in leading states. For a reader evaluating AI relevance, this campus is better positioned to host inference endpoints, regulated enterprise AI applications, or data governance workloads than to train foundation models at scale.
